content: Diseases of affluence are medical conditions that are believed to arise as a consequence of increasing wealth and prosperity within a society. These conditions stand in contrast to diseases of poverty, which are typically associated with impoverishment and lack of resources. Examples of diseases of affluence include Type 2 diabetes, coronary heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, peripheral vascular disease, obesity, certain types of cancer, autoimmune diseases, asthma, alcoholism, depression, and potentially a wide range of other psychiatric disorders. Some of these illnesses are interconnected. For instance, obesity is considered a contributing factor to the development of many other diseases. These conditions are generally classified as non-communicable diseases, whereas diseases of poverty are often communicable. Diseases of poverty are typically spread through infections, inadequate public health infrastructure, poor environmental health conditions, or substandard hygiene practices. As societies experience a decline in starvation and poverty-related diseases, and as life expectancy increases, there is a corresponding rise in the prevalence of diseases of affluence. This shift has led to criticism of policymakers on sociological grounds, as development may be perceived as counterproductive if it results in merely replacing one set of diseases with another. The factors contributing to the rise of diseases of affluence are paradoxical in nature. They are often associated with aspects of life that many people would consider improvements, such as increased access to food, sedentary lifestyles, and other markers of modern living.
